output.title: Why proof-of-concept debt survives
output.body:
Proof-of-concept debt usually survives for one boring reason: the pilot solved a slice of the problem, but nobody made it part of daily work. In this kind of small-business workflow, that often means a manual process is still carrying the load while an unfinished pilot sits on the side.

The decision I’d look at is narrow: does this recurring workflow have a clear owner if you automate it? Not “should we use AI everywhere?”, but “once it works, who runs it day to day?” If the answer is fuzzy, the pilot tends to become shelf-ware. That is just debt with a nicer label.

For an owner-operator, the comparison is simple: keep paying in time and attention for manual work, or invest in one bounded automation that fits a repeatable workflow. Bareni’s diagnostic is built around that question. It identifies one recurring workflow, checks honestly whether AI fits, and, if it does, defines scope, fixed price, and measures. Finished code and accounts stay in the customer’s name from the start; timings are intended scopes, not guarantees.

One practical next step: pick one weekly workflow — customer questions, invoice entry, lead routing, or data sync — and ask who would own it after automation. If you cannot name that person, clarify that before building.
